<reason>Both sides argued well and stayed within closed-book discipline, with no fake sourcing on either side. B framed the stakes memorably ("anonymity is a defect when the product is a date," "stop selling maybe-people") and correctly punished A's initial perfection test with the toll-booth reframe. But A won the analytical spine of the debate by isolating the motion's *distinctive* increment: liveness checks, device/payment signals and photo-hash matching already handle bots, scraped photos and throwaway numbers without costing anonymity, so government-ID deanonymization must be justified by what it adds beyond those. A's pressure questions were the sharpest turn in the debate and extracted two real concessions from B: no badge, no boost, no filter (killing the two-tier design but also conceding the user sees no signal), and that the excluded closeted user is lost as "a real cost of admission" while "the ID is not catching a lie of his." B's remaining route was ban-persistence via attachment, which was a good mechanism, but A's fork then bit: attachment requires durable retention of a document-derived identifier, which is exactly the subpoena/breach/state-demand exposure A had been arguing. B's closing answered that fork by denying "a published citizen file" — a category shift, since A's harm was the record's existence, not publication. That left A's decisive comparison intact: irreversible exposure for the least protected, purchased with a delay for crews already holding fake documents. A's over-limit clipped rebuttal is a real but minor execution cost given the substance landed before the cut.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's retention fork in Rebuttal 2 and Closing: B's ban-persistence benefit requires the company to keep a durable identity-derived record months later, which is precisely the subpoena/leak/government-demand risk B had tried to wave off; B's reply that "remembering doesn't mean a published citizen file" answered publication rather than existence, leaving the fork unbroken.</best_rebuttal>
